6.175.m: Pārvatī said: / O Lord, knower of all reality, by your grace the various duties / pertaining to the glorious Viṣṇu, causes of deliverance for people, have been heard.
Now I also wish to hear the glorification of the Gītā, / by hearing which, O Lord of gods, devotion to Hari increases. / Tell that now, O God, if I am dear to you.
The Lord said: / We worship Mahāviṣṇu, resembling the atasī flower, / seated upon the king of birds, infallible, reclining upon the serpent-couch of Śeṣa.
Once, when the enemy of Mura was seated comfortably on a pleasant seat, / Lakṣmī, who brings joy to the worlds, asked him respectfully.
Śrī said: / You lie asleep in the ocean of milk, O Lord, for what reason, / maintaining the worlds as though indifferent to your sovereign power?
The Lord said: / Hearing this speech of the goddess, the slayer of Mura, proud with knowledge, / spoke in a smooth voice, his eyes smiling with wonder.
The Blessed Lord said: / I am not asleep, O fair-faced one; I perceive my own sovereign form, / with a vision following reality, immersed within.
That which yogins behold within their heart with sharp intellect, O goddess, / and which, as the essence of the Vedas, is deeply contemplated,
that very imperishable light, the nature of the Self, free from disease, / bringing forth a mass of unbroken bliss, devoid of duality,
supported by which the course of the world proceeds and which is experienced by Me, / without which principle nothing in the moving and unmoving world exists,
having churned and thoroughly examined the ocean of the Vedas and treatises in many ways, the wise / Dvaipāyana reached it and brought forth the scripture of the Gītā.
Resting upon that great bliss, my mind made blissful, / I appear as if asleep in the ocean of milk, O ruler of gods.

Having heard those measured, joyful words of that enemy of Mura,
Lakṣmī, her trembling eyes blossoming with delight, was astonished.
Śrī said: / You alone, O Hṛṣīkeśa, are always the object of meditation for self-controlled sages; / therefore, I have great curiosity to hear that which is higher than you.
You yourself are the Lord, the creator and destroyer of the moving and unmoving worlds; / if there is any otherness than the way you abide, instruct me, O Acyuta.
The Blessed Lord said: / This body of mine, O goddess, is made of māyā, not ultimate reality, / magnified by the network of activities of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Distinct from this is the nature of the Self, devoid of duality and non-duality, / free from existence and non-existence, without beginning or end, O beloved.
Obtaining the radiance of pure consciousness, exclusively beautiful with supreme bliss, / that sovereign form accessible through oneness with the Self is proclaimed in the Gītā.

Having heard this speech of the god of immeasurable splendor,
the goddess, feeling doubt regarding the mutually contradictory statements,

'If it is itself supreme bliss, beyond the range of speech and mind, / how does the Gītā make it known? Cut away this doubt of mine.'

The Lord said: / Having heard Śrī's appropriate words, the Lord made known the Gītā, / the vision that follows the Self, along with its legendary history.
'I am the Self, O supreme ruler, twofold by the division of higher and lower: / the higher is the witness, devoid of qualities, without parts, auspicious (Śiva);
the lower is the five-faced one; his condition also is twofold: / by the distinction between word and meaning, he is to be expressed as I, the Self, Maheśvara.
Through the form of the words of the Gītā, that firm bond / of mine, consisting of the objects of worldly existence, is severed.
The five-faced ones and great lords are dependent upon the practice of it.' / Hearing his words from the great ocean of the essence of the Gītā,
this is understood by those who fear worldly existence through its distinction from the higher. / Lakṣmī asked him about this, situated in limbs and minor limbs.
He related the entire glorification along with its legendary history to her. / The Blessed Lord said: / 'Listen, O fair-hipped one, I shall declare the abiding of the Self in the Gītā.
Know the five chapters in succession to be the five faces, / the ten chapters to be the arms, one chapter to be the belly, and two the lotus-feet.
In this way, the eighteen chapters are the sovereign form composed of speech; / it should be known that merely through its knowledge it destroys great sins.
Therefore, the wise person who practices a chapter, or half of it, / or a verse, or half of it, or half of that, is liberated just like Suśarman.'
Śrī said: / 'O God, who was this one named Suśarman, of what caste and what character? / Whence was his liberation, and by what cause did it arise?'
The Blessed Lord said: / 'There was an evil-minded man named Suśarman, the limit of sinful souls, / born in a lineage of Brahmins who did not know the Self and performed cruel deeds.
He had no meditation, no recitation, no fire sacrifice, nor worship of guests; / he occupied himself only with sensual objects, rich in strength.
Ever devoted to agriculture, living off leaves, fond of liquor, / eating meat, in this way he spent a very long time.
Wishing to gather leaves, while wandering in a garden of sages, / he, dull-witted, was bitten there by a deadly serpent.
Meeting the fate of death and going to many hells, / returning once more among mortals, he became an ox.
He was bought by a lame man for the sake of his livelihood; / carrying [loads] on his back, he spent seven or eight years in distress.
Once, driven vigorously for a long time by the lame man, / he suddenly fell to the ground and lapsed into a faint.
With limbs crippled, eyes rolling, and vomiting a stream of foam, / because of his own actions he neither lived nor attained death.
While people were drawn by curiosity to that gathering of folk, / a certain virtuous man transferred merit for his welfare.
Remembering their own actions, some others also gave [merit]. / A certain courtesan standing there, who followed the way of the world,
unaware of her own merit, gave away a little bit. / At first, he was led to the city of the dead by the attendants of Death.
Through the merit given by the courtesan, he was released, considered meritorious. / Returning again to the earthly realm, in a house of virtuous and well-conducted people,
he was born among the twice-born, remembering his previous birth. / After a long time, desiring to know what was beneficial and to dispel his own ignorance,
having approached the courtesan and proclaimed what had been given, he asked [her]. / She explained: "A parrot sitting in a cage recites this daily to me."

"Purified in inner self by that, I assigned that merit [to you]."
Questioned by the two of them, the parrot began to explain,

Remembering a tale of what happened in the past and also his own [former] birth.
The parrot said:
"Formerly, having become a learned man, deluded by pride in my erudition,

Through passion and hatred, envious toward scholars and even toward the virtuous,
In time, dying from there, having reached wretched realms,

I, an extreme reviler of a true guru, was born in the family of parrots;
A doer of wicked deeds during the time of dharma, and separated from my parents.

Brought by eminent sages while heated on the path in the summer heat,
Placed in a cage, I was put in an ashram, an abode of the great.

Hearing the young sons of the sages carefully reciting the first chapter of the Gītā,
I repeatedly practiced its recitation.

Meanwhile, a certain bird-catcher, a perpetrator of thieving deeds,
Seized me and then sold me: thus the event has been related."

The Blessed Lord said:
"This chapter was formerly recited, by which he cast away sin,
By which he became purified in his inner self, and the excellent twice-born was liberated.

Having thus spoken to each other and praised its glorification,
Chanting it day and night, the wise attained liberation in that house.

Therefore, whoever reads, hears, remembers, [or] practices
This first chapter, for him the ocean of existence is not difficult to cross."

6.176.m:
The Blessed Lord said:
"Thus the unexcelled narrative of the first [chapter] has been related.
Hear also the glorification of the other chapters, O Indirā!

In the southern direction, in a city named Puraṃdara,
There was a glorious man of the Vedic reciters, celebrated as Devaśarman,

An honorer of guests, a reciter of scripture, skilled in the Vedas and Śāstras,
A performer of groups of sacrifices, always dear to ascetics.

For a long time he gratified the gods and the fire with offerings,
Yet the righteous-minded one did not obtain absolute peace from that.

Desirous of knowing the supreme good, day after day he served ascetics
Of true resolve, for not a few ages.

As a long time passed while he acted thus,
A certain man freed from karma formerly appeared on earth:

Having experienced, [now] free from desires, his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose,
With tranquil mind, meditating on the supreme Brahman, filled with bliss.

Grasping his feet with a bowed inner self,
The learned man performed the rites of hospitality for him according to rule.

And bowing down with a pure heart, he questioned that satisfied ascetic
Concerning his own state of nirvāṇa.

That knower of the Self said to him, 'In the city named Pura,
There is Mitravant, a goatherd, who will be your instructor.'

Bowing to his feet and going to that mighty city,
In its northern direction he saw an extensive forest,

Charming with the fragrance of many flowers swayed by the wind,
Its directions filled with the humming sounds of impassioned bees.

Then in that forest, on a stone slab on the riverbank, he saw Mitravant
Sitting, joyful, with steady gaze,

Surrounded in the garden shining with the gentle-flowing [river]
By creatures that, casting aside their natural enmity, were mutually hostile,

While herds of deer were tranquil, as if sprinkling nectar upon the ground
With his pleasing bliss of vision, pervaded by compassion.

Approaching him with humility, eager and pleased in mind,
He was honored by him with a slightly inclined head.

Then the learned man, with undivided mind, attended upon Mitravant;
When the time of meditation was ended, composed, he questioned [him]:

Devaśarman said:
'I desire to know the Self; therefore, regarding this wish,
You should instruct me in the means to attain success.'

Mitravant said:
'O learned one, know this past occurrence being spoken by me.

On the bank of the Godāvarī is a city named Pratiṣṭhāna;
There was a man named Durdama in a lineage of wise men.

There is a king named Vikrama being served [there];
Accepting gifts daily, he lived to fill his belly.

In time, bound by the noose of Death, he was taken to the abode of Yama,
And after experiencing tortures in all the hells,

He was born in a certain family of ill-behaved twice-borns;
Endowed with knowledge following him from another existence,

He married an unassailable maiden in a base family.
In time, leaving childhood, she attained youth;

Plump-breasted, with beautiful hips, her eyes bewildered with passion,
She could not tolerate her ill-behaved husband, and desired other husbands instead of her own.

Desiring to earn a livelihood while he had gone outside the city,
She united for a long time with a lustful man born as a Caṇḍāla.

From him she conceived a child, and a girl was born [to her];
She became his very wife due to association with past sin.

In time, having grown old, she became a ḍākinī;
Through bad company and the association with wicked women, she became evil-minded.

Eager for the taste of blood, she devoured a sick hunter;
Wandering in the dreadful forest, having been seen by people, she was banished.

Reaching the realm of the dead, the hunter became a tiger,
After experiencing terrible hells due to the power of harming living beings.

In time, that wicked woman also approached the speed of death;
Going to unassailable hells, she was born as a goat in my house.

Tending her and others in the forest, O learned one,
I saw a dreadful leopard, as if wishing to kill everything.

Seeing him approaching, I, afraid of death,
Fled in fear, abandoning the herd of goats.

Remembering former enmity, the leopard attacked;
And the goat went near him, swiftly, near the river.

There, shedding fear, unhindered, casting aside enmity,
She stood; and the leopard remained silent, free from malice.

Seeing him like that, she began to speak:
'O leopard, having raised me up respectfully, do you not eat the desired meat?

This disposition is not yours; how is it that you have cast off hostile thoughts?'
Hearing that speech, the leopard, free from malice, then said:

'In this place my hatred has departed, and hunger and thirst have vanished;
Therefore I do not seek you who are present nearby.'

Thus addressed, she spoke again: 'How have I become fearless?
Do you know what the reason is here? If so, you should tell me.'

Thus addressed, the leopard again said to her, 'I do not know, O goat;
Let us go to ask this great one who has come before us.' Thus the two set out.

Having approached, I was questioned by both of them, filled with great wonder;
And accompanied by the two of them, I questioned the lord of monkeys.

Questioned by me, O twice-born, the monkey respectfully said this:
'Hear, O goatherd, I shall tell the ancient event here.

Behold this great temple situated in the forest ahead;
Here indeed is the liṅga of Tryambaka, consecrated by Druhiṇa.

An intelligent man named Sukarma, practicing austerity, worships
The [liṅga] facing east, adorable to the gods, having brought wild flowers.'
Bathing [the Liṅga] with river waters and living solely through [his] work, / after a long time, a certain guest came into his presence.
Bringing food made of fruits, he offered [it] to him. / Delighted with that hospitality, [the guest] spoke to Sukarman:
"Why do you remain engaged, having enjoyed the fruit whose root is this action? / Or do you strive merely out of blind imitation?"
Being addressed thus mostly by that delighted knower of the Self, / [Sukarman] then replied with clear speech that was supremely beneficial to himself:
"O learned one, I do not truly know the fruit of this action, / by which Śambhu, the Supreme, is served merely out of a desire to know.
The culmination and fruit of this service to Kapardin [Śiva] / is that you favor me, fulfilling the desire of my heart."
Hearing his truthful words, the ascetic was delighted, / and he inscribed the second chapter of the Gītā upon a stone slab.
He quickly instructed the Brahmin to recite and study it: / "Your heart's desire will freely bear fruit in every way."

Having spoken thus, the wise one disappeared before his very eyes as he watched;
and amazed, at his command he practiced continuously.
Then, after a long time, with a purified soul and a serene intellect, / wherever he roamed, that ascetic grove became peaceful.

There is no affliction of pairs of opposites, neither hunger, thirst, nor fear;
know this to be by the ascetic power of that reciter of the second chapter.
Mitravān said: / Having been addressed thus by him, after telling that supreme story, / permitted by that gracious one, I departed accompanied by the she-goat and the tiger.
Having gone, seeing on the stone slab the inscribed chapter, one should recite it; / by its very repetition, the supreme end of penance was attained.
Therefore, O auspicious one, you too ought to recite that chapter daily; / through it, your liberation will not be far away.
Devaśarman, thus instructed personally by that Mitravān, / having worshipped and bowed down, went to the city of Puraṃdara [Indra].
There, having approached a knower of the Self in a temple of the gods, / having first reported this occurrence, he then recited the chapter.
Instructed by him, purified in soul, reciting the second chapter with reverence, / he attained the exalted, flawless supreme state.
This narrative of the second [chapter] has been told; now listen. / And I shall speak, O Indirā, of the glorification of the third.

6.177.m: The Blessed Lord said: / In Janasthāna there was a twice-born named Jaḍa belonging to the Kauśika lineage, / who, abandoning the duty appropriate to his caste, set his mind on the livelihood of a merchant.
Addicted to the wives of others, gambling with dice, drinking liquor, / and constantly devoted to hunting, he thus passed his time.
Then, when his wealth was exhausted, he took to theft by night; / by that means, he seized the wealth of sacrificers who wished to perform sacrifices.
With that [wealth] he went far to the northern direction for trade, / having taken musk, black aloe, and chowries radiant as moonlight,
and having turned back, he brought [it] five or six yojanas along the way. / Then, on another day, desiring intensely to see his beloved,
having traversed a long distance, when the sun had set / and darkness spread at will across the ten directions, at the foot of a tree,
he fell into the power of bandits and was swiftly slain by them. / Due to the loss of dharma he was born as a terrifying and most ferocious evil spirit,
thirsty, afflicted with hunger, licking the corners of his mouth, / with hair standing erect, extremely long-shanked, his belly sticking to his back, huge,
having a body of mere bones, with wildly rolling eyes. / In the meantime, his son, righteous and versed in the Vedas,
waited anxiously, desiring to see him; then he went [forth]. / Constantly seeking news from travelers, he obtained none.
Then at one time, when a companion had arrived, / having learned the account from him, he grieved greatly for his father.
Then, having reflected, the wise [son], wishing to perform the rites for the next world, / having gathered provisions, set out to go to Vārāṇasī.
Having spent seven or eight nights on the path, at the foot of that tree / where his father had been slain, he began to perform the twilight worship.
There he recited the third chapter of the Gītā. / Then a terrible sound echoed in the midst of the sky.
Then he saw his terrible father falling from the sky; / with his mind bewildered by astonishment and fear,
he saw [the space] before him in the sky filled with immense splendor; / crowded with millions of small bells, filling the directions with radiance,
he saw ahead a celestial aerial chariot, his intellect [now] sharp. / There he saw [his father] mounted upon it, surrounded by celestial women,
praised by sages, wearing yellow garments. / Having bowed down and looked upon him, he was embraced by him with a blessing.
Then he asked about this event, and [the father] reported to him: / "From that body difficult to abandon due to karma, by the cause of merit,
I have been liberated by you reciting the chapter nearby by good fortune. / Therefore return from reciting; now that which has approached you,

that for the sake of which you would go to Vārāṇasī, has been accomplished for yourself."
The Blessed Lord said:
Thus addressed, he spoke to his father of blazing splendor.

The Blessed Lord said:
Then the father said to his son: "This is to be done by you, sinless one.
The deed that was done by me was also done by my brother; / he has gone to a dreadful hell; you ought to liberate him.
And whatever others in my lineage have reached hell, / they too are to be liberated; this is my wish."

Addressed in this manner, the son, with hands folded in reverence, spoke to him again:
"By what action may I deliver them all? Instruct that [to me]."

Thus addressed in speech, the father spoke to his son.
The father said:
"By that by which I was liberated, child, that you ought to practice.
Having practiced it, release to them the merit born from that. / Then, like me, all those ancestors, abandoning their torment,

will go before long to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
Having been thus instructed, the son spoke: "If it is so, father, / then I will liberate all the hell-dwellers, if this word pleases you."

"May it be so! May there be welfare! A great delight has come about."
Having thus instructed his son, the father went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Having thus instructed his son, the father went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
and he too, having turned back from there, reached Janasthāna and
passed his time in the temple of Śauri, before the Beautiful One. / Performing the equinoxes and other rites, and what was spoken by his father,
he released the merit he had performed, wishing to liberate the hell-dwellers. / In the meantime, messengers, about to liberate the hell-dwellers,
who had reached the state of torment, to the abode of Viṣṇu, approached Yama. / By him they were all honored with multifaceted acts of hospitality;
asked about their welfare, they spoke of happiness on all sides. / Having honored them, the wise great lord of the realm of the ancestors
asked the reason for their coming, and they reported to him: / "Know, lord of Kīnāśa, that we have been dispatched by Śauri,
who reclines on the bed of Śeṣa, to deliver an order into your presence. / Through our mouth the God inquires after your welfare,
and directs you to release all living beings who dwell in hell." / Having heard this command of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
honoring it with bowed head, he meditated on something in his mind. / Having seen all those released from hell, proud and exhilarated,
he, followed by them all, went in an excellent vehicle to the abode of Viṣṇu, / where the milk ocean lies.
There he beheld the teacher of the world, equal in radiance to millions of risen suns, / dark as the petal of a blue lotus,
whose splendor was mixed with the rays from the jewels on the hoods of the serpent bed, / who was being looked upon, full of bliss, with a delighted mind,
gazed upon repeatedly with love by Śrī with charming glances following her affection, / attended all around by yogins whose pupils were motionless in meditation,
praised by Mahendra in order to vanquish his adversaries, / at the conclusion of the words of the Vedas uttered from the mouth of Brahmā,
whose multitude of virtues was sung by embodied words, / both delighted and yet indifferent in all wombs,
simultaneously [witnessing] the merits gathered by yoga among living beings, / beholding himself as the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings,
gladdening himself with glances filled with radiance, / bearing an all-pervading form illuminated by the brilliance of the serpent,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, as the sky is [illuminated] by moonlight. / Seeing him, he, bowing down with abundant devotion, praised [him].

Yama said:
"Salutations to the Creator of universal form, whose mind is purified through creating all things, / from whose mouth the Vedas were uttered!
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the support of the universe, the sattva [quality] in preservation, / who destroys the pride of the lords of the Dānavas difficult to withstand in force and speed!
Salutations to [him who is] victorious over the mass of sins of all embodied beings, / whose flames arise from the fire of the forehead eye slightly opening!
For you are the teacher, the soul, the great lord of all the world; / having abandoned all the Vaiṣṇavas, you therefore show compassion.
Pervading the entire world expanded by māyā, / you are not overcome by it, nor by the guṇas born from it.
Even dwelling within, you are not overwhelmed by those two; / even with a mind intending to restrain through a vision dwelling in objects of sense,
through that [vision] reaching the fruits, you dissolve into yourself alone. / There is no end to your greatness, just as you are yourself limitless.

Silence alone is proper for me here; how are you an object of words?"
Having praised [him] thus, he then spoke this word with folded hands:
"By your command, these embodied beings, devoid of qualities, have been released by me. / Command what other duty there is for me, teacher of the world."

Having been petitioned by him in this manner, Madhusūdana spoke to him
with a voice deep as a thundercloud, as if sprinkling [him] with the nectar of ambrosia:
"The world is delivered from sin by me abiding by the proper order; / with the burden placed upon you, I do not grieve for embodied beings."
"Therefore, perform your own duty and go to your own home." / The Blessed Lord said: / Having spoken thus, the god vanished, and he too went to his own city.
He too, having rescued his own kinsmen who were in hell in large numbers, / himself went to the realm of Viṣṇu in an excellent vehicle.

6.178.m: The Blessed Lord said: / Now I shall tell the glorification of the fourth [chapter] as well; listen, / through which two maidens, abandoning their state as jujube trees, went to heaven.
Śrī said: / How did the two maidens go to heaven, having shed their state as jujube trees? / And who were they formerly, O Lord, and how did they attain pre-eminence?
I wish to know this, O Lord; you ought to tell [me], / for I am never sated while listening to this supreme narrative.
The Blessed Lord said: / On the bank of the Bhāgīrathī there is a city named Vārāṇasī. / There, in the temple of Viśveśvara, a self-controlled ascetic named Bharata,

Ever delighting in the Self, he attentively recites the fourth chapter;
from that repeated practice, the uncorrupted soul is not overcome by pairs of opposites.
Once upon a time, sporting, he went outside the city; / desiring to see the gods dwelling on the outskirts, that rich in penance
rested at the foot of two jujube trees whose fruits were falling down, / resting his head on one of them and supporting his feet on the other.
Then, when the ascetic had departed, the pair of jujube trees / withered and became bare of leaves and branches in five or six days.
Then in the house of a Brahmin, two maidens were born; / growing up, the pair of them, after seven years,
after roaming from distant regions, saw the ascetic coming. / Taking hold of his feet, they spoke truthful words:

"By your favor alone, O sage, the pair of us has been liberated;
casting off the state of being jujube trees, [this one] attains human form."
Being spoken to thus by the two of them, the sage, who had forgotten, replied: / 'When, my daughters, and for what reason were you two released by me?
And tell me the cause of your state as jujube trees; I do not know.' / The two maidens spoke to him of the cause of their own jujube state,
and first the cause of their liberation from that which was hard to escape: / 'On the bank of the Godāvarī there is a sacred ford that bestows merit upon men,
renowned as Chhinnapāpa ("Severed Sin"), which grants the highest state. / There, [a sage] named Satyatapas performed severe penance.
In the great summer heat, standing in the midst of blazing fires; / in the rainy seasons, his matted hair constantly drenched with torrents of water;
and in the cold season, dwelling in water, bearing a bristling body— / ever purified, having performed penance at all times, that self-restrained one
fixed his mind thus on the Self, attaining supreme tranquility. / Even while bearing supreme love toward trees always laden with fruit and thick with shade,
and toward beings free of malice, / he did not set his mind on pursuing the fruits of penance on account of his wisdom.
Even Brahmā, asking him personally, attended upon him every day; / through that, being free from hesitation, he was daily devoted to the Absolute.
The penance of him whose manifestation was devoted to that meditation increased. / Thinking himself almost liberated from his prosperous post,
Puraṃdara, terrified because of this, created a hundred obstacles. / Summoning the two of us from among the apsarases, he commanded us equally:
'Do you two obstruct that penance undertaken by him, / who wishes to enjoy my own kingdom after dislodging me from my station!'

When this message was delivered before Biḍaujas,
we two went to the Godāvarī, where that sage resides.
With mṛdaṅga drums sounding deep and slow, and with flutes playing sweet tones, / sweet singing was begun, accompanied by slender-bodied maidens.
[We two], bearing broad hips and firm, plump breasts, / with lotus faces smiling gently, with locks of hair slightly curled,
our shoulders touched by jeweled earrings, our eyes radiant like white lotuses, / slender-waisted, with well-rounded thighs, moving with matching steps,
danced for the sake of youthful love in accordance with notes, rhythm, and tempo, / displaying by nature every movement expressive of emotional states.

Originating with gentle steps, gradually and slowly increasing,
that [dance] of the two dancing made the circle of the directions resound.

Then, through the speed of the body movements, a very cool breeze shook [their] garments;
as their clothes slipped slightly, displaying their breasts,

the intense motion of the two of us, exciting passion,
aroused anger in the sage whose mind had been undisturbed.

Then, out of wrath, releasing water with his hand, he gave a curse:
'May both of you become jujube trees on the bank of the Jāhnavī!'

Afterward, the sage was appeased by the two bowing down humbly:
'Whatever misdeed was committed by us two under another’s command, forgive that!'

Then the sage of virtuous intellect appointed our release from the curse,
speaking truly: 'This [curse] shall end with the arrival of Bharata;

and [there shall be] an acquisition of birth among mortals and the remembrance of past lives.
Then, going near the two of us who had become jujube trees,

you, reciting the fourth chapter, brought about our deliverance.
Therefore, we bow down to you; not only from the curse,

but from terrible saṃsāra itself have we two been liberated by you.'
The Blessed Lord said:
Being spoken to thus by the two, the sage, having an exceedingly delighted mind,

honored by them and taking leave, went away as he had come.
May the two maidens daily recite the fourth chapter with reverence!

6.179.m:
The Blessed Lord said:
Now, O goddess, I shall relate in brief the glorification of the fifth chapter,
which is revered by the world; listen attentively, O beloved!

In the country of Bhadra, in the city of Purukutsa, there was a twice-born named Piṅgala,
born in a spotless and renowned family of exponents of the Veda.

Abandoning the scriptures appropriate to his family as well as the Vedas,
he turned his mind to the triple arts of song, dance, and music, playing drums and other instruments.

Having exerted himself there in singing, dancing, and instrumental music,
and attaining supreme renown, he entered the king's palace.

Formerly he associated with that king as an equal;
stealing the wives of others, he enjoyed them, single-minded [in lust].

Then he became haughty and arrogant, unbridled in speaking malicious words,
and in secret he constantly revealed the faults of others to him.
He had a wife named Aruṇā, born of a low caste.

Wandering about in search [of pleasure], sporting with a lover,
she, regarding [her husband] as an obstacle, in the middle of the night in her own dwelling,

slew him by cutting off his head and buried him in the earth.
Deprived of his life-breaths, he went to the abode of Yama.

After suffering in hells difficult to overcome, he became a vulture in a deserted forest.
She too, casting off her body through the disease of fistula,

entered terrible hells and was born there in that forest as a female parrot.
As she was wandering here and there, desiring to eat grain,

the vulture, remembering the enmity, tore her with sharp claws.
Then, as the female parrot fell into a human skull filled with water,

the vulture also rushed at her, and he was struck down by bird-catchers.
Then the wife was deprived of life in the water of that human skull,

and arriving there, that very cruel bird also plunged [into it] and died.
Led by the servants of Yama, the two reached the realm of the ancestors,
sharing fear and remembering their former evil deeds.

Then Yama, seeing their loathsome karma,
and the great merit [acquired] suddenly by that bath at the time of death,

permitted the two to go to the world they desired,
even though their minds were intractable with an accumulation of great sins.

Then, filled with wonder, remembering their own evil deeds,
the two approached, bowed down, and questioned Vaivasvata:

'Previously, a despised evil deed was accumulated by both of us;
what is the cause of our reaching the desired worlds? Tell that to us two!'

Being addressed thus by the two, Vaivasvata then spoke these words:
'There was [a sage] on the bank of the Gaṅgā who, having known the eternal Brahman,

solitary, devoid of possessiveness, tranquil, free from passion, and devoid of envy,
was always reciting the fifth chapter of the Gītā.

Purified in self by that merit, having known the eternal Brahman,
he shed his body, upon hearing which even a sinner is purified.

Attaining the water in the skull of that one whose body was cleansed
and whose self was permeated by the Gītā, you two have attained purity.

Therefore, go to the worlds lying in the path of your desires,
purified by the glorification of the fifth chapter of the Gītā.'

Enlightened in this way by that Equitable One, delighted,
they mounted a celestial vehicle and went to the realm of Viṣṇu.

6.180.m:
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall proclaim the glorification of the sixth chapter, O fair-faced one,
upon hearing which liberation rests in the palm of men's hands.

On the bank of the Godāvarī there is a great city named Pratiṣṭhāna,
where I dwell under the name Pippaleśa, O bright-eyed one;

where swans, with their spread wing-tips, remove the fatigue of ascetics
by means of the cool spray from the bank of the Godāvarī;

where the praiseworthy water of the Godāvarī, perfumed by the pollen from the clusters of blossoming lotuses,
makes men immortal deities through its use;

where foremost sages touch the faces of bathing Mahārāṣṭra brides,
mistaking them for full-blown lotuses, crying 'fie on the nectar of the moon that causes affliction and wanes!';

where the sounds of the charmingly jingling bangles of sporting Mahārāṣṭra women
captivate even the minds of absorbed ascetics;

where the hare-marked moon, beholding day after day the faces of women
strolling on the tops of very lofty mansions, wanes [out of shame];

where [the roofs] are kissed by the rays of great jewels on the balconies of exceedingly high palaces,
flickering like dūrvā grass and sandalwood, [visited] by sages and gandharvas;

in which city the chariot-horses of the sun have their fatigue removed
by the breezes from the fluttering banners;

in which the Malaya mountain seems to be left with only stones,
because of the countless heaps of sandalwood piled up by merchants;

and where even heaps of pearls are seen
like bunches of smiles of the city’s presiding deity all around.

There was a king there named Jānaśruti,
while whom protecting the earth resembling a crest-jewel on Śeṣa,

whose majesty was fierce like the disc of the blazing sun,
the wish-fulfilling trees, perpetually blackened by the sacrificial smoke,
withered from shame, seeing his extraordinary generosity;

longing for the taste of chewing the sacrificial rice-cakes of his sacrifices,
the gods never abandoned the city of Pratiṣṭhāna even for a moment;

nourished by the streams of water of his donations, by the moonlight of his glory at night,
and by the smokes of his sacrifices, the clouds poured rain in season;

calamities never found even the slightest footing anywhere,
and moral policies flourished while he ruled the earth;

who, under the guise of reservoirs, wells, and ponds, daily
beheld the treasures dwelling within the heart of the earth;

whose palace shone with white banners,
like the peak of the Himālaya with the torrents of the celestial Gaṅgā's waves.
Pleased by his gifts, austerities, sacrifices, and protection of his subjects, / the dwellers of heaven came together to grant him a boon.
Then, flapping their multitude of wings along the path of the atmosphere, / divine swans, radiant and white as lotus stalks, set out.
As they were flying swiftly, conversing among themselves there, / two or three, led by Bhadrāśva, dashed ahead with speed.
As they all came together, they spoke to those flying ahead in haste: / 'Why have you rushed forward with such speed and taken your stand in front?
All must travel together on this impassable path. / Do you not see the mass of splendour blazing before you,
which belongs to King Jānaśruti, an embodiment of merit, so distinctly visible?' / Having heard these words of those behind, those in front,
the swans, laughed contemptuously and spoke these words aloud: / 'Can the glory of this king, Jānaśruti, indeed be more intense
than the unassailable splendour of the knower of Brahman named Raikva?' / King Jānaśruti heard these words of the swans
as he sat at ease, having ascended his lofty palace mansion. / Then, struck with wonder, the king summoned his charioteer,
and that noble soul commanded: 'Let Raikva be brought here!' / Thereupon, hearing the king's command filled with nectar-like words,
the charioteer, Mahān by name, set out, spreading delight. / [He went] where the city named Vārāṇasī, granter of liberation, lies,
where the Lord of the Universe, named Viśveśvara, is the teacher; / then to the sacred place named Gayā, where Lord Gadādhara,
with wide-open eyes, resides to deliver all the worlds; / then beside the father of Gaurī, [passing] in various ways through all the holy sites,
wandering, he went to where Kedāra, the tearer of sin, resides, / by seeing whom mortals become liberated once and for all—of this there is no doubt—
freed from great sins, after enjoying their desired pleasures. / Then he went to Gauḍa, where Puruṣottama abides,
merely by beholding whom men become goers to the heavenly world. / Then he went to Dvārāvatī, the city that grants liberation,
where Hari, the beloved of Rukmiṇī, resides on the bank of the Gomatī. / Having bathed in the Gomatī tīrtha and beheld the five Kṛṣṇas,
a mortal attains liberation after enjoying his desired pleasures. / Then, reaching the ocean and beholding Somanātha,
the god who grants enjoyment and liberation, the wise man departed thence. / He reached the city Avantikā, which bestows enjoyment and liberation,
where Śaṅkara Mahākāla sports happily with Umā. / Then, having reached Oṅkāra on the bank of the Narmadā, who grants peace / and bestows enjoyment and liberation, he departed in haste from there.
Then, wandering to the city named Aśvamedhakara, / where the Wielder of the Śārṅga Bow, the Lord of Lakṣmī Himself, resides in visible form;
then he reached Viṣṇugayā, the pool named Loṇāra, / bathing and drinking where a man is freed from bondage.
Then he went to the place named Kolhāpura, towards Rudragayā, / where the divine Lakṣmī, the bestower of devotion, resides.
Having bathed in the Pañcanadī and beheld Mahālakṣmī, / a man enjoys pleasures as he desires and obtains devotion.
Then, having reached the city named Amalagiri, / where Somanātha is mounted upon Nandikeśvara,
and having seen the four-armed god, the auspicious Somanātha intent on giving boons, / liberation is certain for men—of this there is no doubt.
Then, having seen Harihara on the bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā River, / whose arms fall upon the earth in cosmic age after cosmic age,
and beholding that charming form of Harihara, / all men enjoy pleasures according to their desire and are freed from bondage;
having dwelt in heaven for a hundred kalpas, they are freed from the bonds of saṃsāra. / Then, having seen the Lord, the all-pervading Master of the worlds,
beholding whom men never see hell, / and having dwelt in heaven for a hundred kalpas, freed from the latent impressions of saṃsāra,
they obtain liberation; no doubt should be entertained here. / Then, having reached Śrīśaila, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
where the beloved of Girijā, known by the name Mallinātha, [resides] / in order to deliver all worlds from the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra,
having dwelt in heaven for a hundred kalpas, freed from the bonds of saṃsāra, / they obtain liberation; no doubt should be entertained here.
Then, having reached Śrīśaila, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas, / where the beloved of Girijā, known by the name Mallinātha, [resides]
in order to deliver all worlds from the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra, / who Himself reveals the supreme light from age to age;
for men who behold Him and even for those who remember Him, / the torments of hell, terrified, stay far away.
Having enjoyed happiness in the heavenly world, freed from the bonds of saṃsāra, / humans attain liberation—of this there is no doubt.
Rāma with his younger brother along with Sītā is also there, to which he went; / having bathed and drunk there, one is surely freed from hell.
Having enjoyed the bliss of the heavenly world for a hundred crore kalpas, / men whose path in saṃsāra has ended attain liberation—of this there is no doubt.
Turning back from there, he came, beholding on the bank of the Bhīmarathī / the two-armed god Viṭhṭhala, who grants enjoyment and liberation.
Where the great Brahmagiri is, the birthplace of the Godāvarī, / he reached the hermitage of Gautama, where Hara Tryambaka resides;
where between the Aruṇā and Varuṇā is the river Godāvarī, / bathing and drinking there, [the sin of] murdering a brahmin is dissolved.
Having seen Brahmagiri endowed with countless holy places, / men attain liberation alone, freed from the sorrow of saṃsāra.
Curious to seek out the holy places located on both banks of the Gautamī, / the charioteer then went to Mathurā, which destroys sins,
where gods and humans worship the self-manifest Lord, / the primordial abode of the Blessed Lord, the great bestower of liberation,
the birthplace of the Lord of the three worlds, celebrated in the Vedas and Śāstras, / frequented by hosts of various deities and served by assemblies of twice-born seers,
adorned by the banks of the Kālindī, having the shape of a half-moon, / the sole residence of all holy places, filled with beauty and bliss,
bearing the sacred Govardhana hill, covered with sacred trees and creepers, / having the highly meritorious twelve forests, possessing the essence of the Vedic resting-place.
Then he saw the city of Kāśmīra to the north-west, / having seen Kurukṣetra, the sacred field bearing the burden of dharma on all sides,
where the rows of cloud-scraping mansions, white as conch shells, / appeared distinctly like the loud laughter of Dhūrjaṭi,
surrounded by golden pinnacles on rows of temples, / like golden lotuses fallen from the celestial river by the winds;
where on the spires of the palaces the blue silk banners / shine like masses of moss and creepers of the celestial river;
where Sarasvatī dwells perpetually, taking refuge in Kāśmīra— / otherwise, how could she simultaneously write all this literature?—
where the swans with lotus-stalk beaks, languid with joy, / her vehicles, roam for a long time while Sarasvatī rests.

where swans arrived from all around, sent by Brahmā
to learn a particular art, shone like stars;

where land-lotuses, pleasing to the touch of hands,
were seen arranged by the enemy of the Dānavas as a bed for his broad-hipped wife;

where, through the expositions of the twice-born, a mute deity,
with words resounding in billows of syllables, is clearly not heard;

where the vault of the sky, pervaded by sacrificial smoke,
does not lose its blackness, even though washed by clouds;

where, by the guise of the cool-rayed moon's spot,
one sees the mark made by the great sacrificial flame when ambrosia trickled down;

where young pupils, solely by the power of study in a former birth,
themselves read all the arts upon approaching a teacher;

where the tinkling sound of the bracelets of Brahmins' wives
daily drowns out the buzzing of wandering bees;

where the gentle breeze constantly touches the cheeks of the Brahmins' wives,
blowing softly, as if in fear of a curse;

where that moon-crested god, named Māṇikyeśvara,
dwells continually to bestow boons upon embodied souls;

having been worshipped after conquering kings and honored by Maṇikeśa,
from that time onward he bore the name Māṇikyeśvara;

because he was worshipped lavishly with rubies
by the king, the lord of Kaśmīra, when celebrating his conquest of the directions;

there the charioteer saw Raikya enjoying that water
under the shade upon a cart, scratching his limbs.

Instantly recognized by the various signs described by the king,
the charioteer bowed low, prostrated to Raikya, and addressed him.

The charioteer said:
'In what [place], O Brahmin, and what is your name? You are ever unfettered.
For what purpose have you rested here, and what do you intend to do?'

Having heard that speech, filled with supreme joy,
and remembering his charioteer, he said: "Our desires are fulfilled."

Yet someone must perform abundant service for us,
knowing indeed our state of mind.'

Taking to heart Raikya's intention with reverence,
the charioteer departed slowly to where the lord of the earth resided.

Then, having bowed to the ruler of the earth, he reported what had occurred,
folding his hands in reverence, delighted at the sight of his master.

Upon hearing his words, his eyes smiling with wonder,
the king became full of faith in honoring Raikya.

Taking a cart yoked with a pair of mules,
pearl necklaces, fine garments, and a thousand cows, the king set out.

He went to that place in the region of Kaśmīra where the yogi dwelt;
offering that before him, the king fell upon the ground like a rod.

Though bowed with supreme devotion, Raikya became angry with the king:
'O Śūdra! You do not know my conduct, you wretched lord!

Take back this cart yoked with mules, and take yourself
the garments, pearl necklaces, and the milch cows!'

Speaking thus, he struck fear into the king.
Then, terrified of a curse, the king, taking hold of his two lotus-feet
with devotion, himself said, 'Be gracious, O Brahmin!'

The king said:
'O venerable one, whence is this most wonderful greatness of yours?
Becoming gracious, O Lord, tell me in truth.'

Raikya said:
'I recite the sixth chapter of the Gītā daily, O king.
By that alone is my mass of splendor unbearable even to the gods.'

Having diligently studied the sixth chapter of the Gītā from Raikya,
the wise king Jānaśruti obtained liberation from that.

Raikya too attained happiness in the presence of Māṇikyeśvara,
reciting the sixth chapter of the Gītā, which bestows liberation.

Having assumed the guise of swans, they came to grant boons;
the denizens of heaven, filled with wonder, also departed at their pleasure.

Whatever person recites even this single chapter constantly,
he too attains the abode of Viṣṇu, without doubt.

6.181.m:
The Holy One said:
'Now I shall describe to you the majesty of the seventh chapter,
hearing which a flood of nectar fills the ears.

There is a fortress named Pāṭaliputra with towering gateway towers.
There lived a Brahmin named Śaṅkukarṇodayārṇava.

Adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, he acquired much wealth;
he did not offer libations to the ancestors, nor did he worship the gods.

Devoted to acquiring wealth, he fed kings.
For the sake of auspiciousness, to take a fourth wife into his household,

he once set out along with his sons and relatives.
At night, which was like a duty to him, while he was asleep, under his arm

a venomous serpent, arriving from somewhere, bit him.
As soon as he was bitten, incurable through jewels, mantras, herbs, and the like,

in just a few moments his life-breath departed.
Covering his body with nimba leaves and stalks,

the sons placed it in the crook of a tree and returned home.
Then, after a long time, he was born there as a reptile.

Bound by the latent impressions of that former birth, remembering it,
[he thought,] 'Deceiving these sons, I shall fill [my hoard] outside the house,'

where his wealth numbering in crores was buried.
Then, endowed with supreme faith, the sons of the twice-born performed

the Nārāyaṇabali rite for the deceased.
Once, appearing in a dream, afflicted by his birth as a serpent,

the father revealed the state of his mind before his sons.
Then, rising in the morning, filled with supreme wonder,

they told one another and became completely unrestrained.
One of them, out of filial affection, wished to deliver him;

another, out of greed for wealth, sought to kill the serpent;
and another, his mind bewitched by the sentiment of affection for his father,

merely wept, lamenting, 'Why should he have become a serpent?'
Then the middle son, deceiving his two brothers,

rose up under some pretext and went to his own home.
Then, having softly summoned his virtuous wife,

he went out with a spade in his hand to where his serpent father dwelt.
Not knowing the wealth, but determining [the place] accurately by signs,

he went to the spot with a greedy mind to kill him at the anthill.
The earth was removed by his wife, and he dug it up himself.

From the anthill that was being dug out, a terrifying serpent arose.
Then, with unbearable gushes of poison issuing forth,
the serpent spoke words amidst blasts of hissing wind.

The serpent said:
'Who are you? Why have you come? Why is this hole being dug?
By whom have you been sent, fool? Tell that before me!'

[The serpent] said:
Hearing this word of his son, which was condemned by the world,
the serpent then began to speak clearly, laughing aloud.

The son said:
O father, tell me how your liberation may come to be,
[since] leaving all people behind, I have come [here] at night.

The father said:
Neither sacred bathing sites, nor gifts, nor austerities, nor sacrifices,
O son, are in any way able to release me,

Except for the nectar-like seventh chapter of the Gītā,
which is the cause for eradicating old age, death, and suffering for an embodied being.

Feed with faith, O son, on the day of my śrāddha,
a Brahmin who recites the seventh chapter; by that, liberation [will come], no doubt.

Feed also other twice-borns skilled in the lore of the Vedas,
according to your capacity, endowed with the highest faith.

Having heard that command of their father, who had attained the condition of a serpent,
all those sons did as instructed, and even more than that.

Then the illustrious Śaṅkukarṇa, casting off his serpent body,
made a division [of his wealth] among his sons and assumed a celestial body.

With the wealth, numbered in the tens of millions, divided and given by their father,
all those sons of righteous conduct rejoiced.

For the sake of step-wells, wells, ponds, sacrifices, and temples of the gods,
those sons, of righteous intellect, then built an almshouse.

From the recitation of the seventh chapter, they then attained liberation;
having known the sixth as most dear, their sight was fixed on final release.

6.182.m:
Śiva said:
Listen to the glorification of the eighth chapter, which I shall declare, O Pārvatī,
by the mere hearing of which you will attain supreme delight.

There was a city named Āmardaka, renowned in the southern land;
there lived a twice-born named Bhāvaśarman, the keeper of a courtesan,

eating meat, drinking liquor, stealing the property of righteous men,
delighting in other men's wives, and fond of hunting.

Exceedingly cruel, he pursued his vast desire,
and in the assembly of rogues, with his companions, [he drank] the sweet nectar of the palmyra fruit.

Having drunk up to his throat, afflicted by severe indigestion,
that evil-minded man died in time and became a great palmyra tree.

Resorting to its shade, which was dense and very cool,
a certain husband and wife, who had fallen into the state of brahmarākṣasas, stayed.

The Goddess said:
Of what caste were they, what was their nature, and of what conduct? Tell this!
Or by what deed, O lord, did they attain the state of brahmarākṣasas?

Śiva said:
There was a certain twice-born named Kuśīvala, of virtuous conduct,
who knew the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas and was skilled in the meaning of all śāstras.

And his wife, named Kumati, was evil-minded.
Together with his wife, he accepted great gifts, being excessively greedy.

Day after day [he accepted] a buffalo, a kālapuruṣa image, horses, and the like,
not giving even a single cowrie obtained from gifts to twice-borns.

In time, both husband and wife died and became brahmarākṣasas,
wandering over this earth, their bodies agitated by hunger and thirst.

Then, having arrived, they rested at the root of that palmyra tree.
"How may this great suffering of ours depart?

Or how can liberation arise from the womb of a brahmarākṣasa?"
Asked thus by his housewife, that Brahmin spoke:

"Without the instruction in the knowledge of brahman, without reflection on the supreme self,
[and] without knowledge of the rules of action, how can one be freed from distress?"

The wife said:
"What is that brahman? What is the supreme self? What is action, O Supreme Person?"
Listen to what wonder took place when this much had been spoken by his wife!

From hearing that half-verse of the eighth chapter, that tree then
abandoned the form of a palmyra and became an excellent twice-born.

Instantly his self was purified by knowledge, freed from the slough of sin;
and by that glorification, the husband and wife were also completely liberated.

This much alone was spoken, having emerged by chance from his mouth.
Then, arriving from the sky, a beautiful [aerial chariot], with tinkling bells,

adorned in heaven by the moon-like faces of celestial maidens,
and filled with bees roaming around the lotus-like faces of Apsarases,

bright with fly-whisks white as the foam on the shore of the churned milk-ocean
and lovely as the waves of the Gaṅgā,

charming with singing Gandharvas and a hundred dancing wives of the gods—
mounting that divine aerial chariot, the husband and wife went to heaven.

All this wondrous occurrence that took place there—
then the wise [Bhāvaśarman] carefully wrote down this half-verse.

He went to the city named Vārāṇasī, the giver of liberation,
desiring to worship the god of gods, Janārdana.

There, of supremely noble mind, he began to practice austerities.
In the meantime, Janārdana, the god of gods, the Lord of the Universe,

was questioned by the daughter of the milk-ocean, having joined the hollow of her hands:
"Why do you remain having abandoned the path of sleep? Let this be told!"

The Holy One said:
In Kāśī, on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, a twice-born performs severe austerity,
Bhāvaśarman, very intelligent, filled with the nectar of devotion to me,

reciting half a verse of the eighth chapter of the Gītā, his senses restrained.
I am exceedingly pleased, O goddess, with his austerity.

Reflecting for a long time, my mind is eager to give him
a reward worthy of that austerity, O beloved, as I dwell [here] now.

Pārvatī said:
If Hari, though pleased, attained anxiety, O Lord,
did Bhāvaśarman, the devotee of Hari, then obtain that reward?

Bhāvaśarman, the best of the twice-born, attained ultimate bliss,
and all the descendants of his lineage also attained that high state.

Even those who formerly had attained torment by the power of their deeds [were saved].
Just this much of the glorification of the eighth chapter has been told to you,
O fawn-eyed one; it is always to be contemplated.

6.183.m:
There is a city named Māhiṣmatī on the bank of the Narmadā;
there lived a twice-born named Mādhava, a Brahmin dedicated to Śiva,

knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, fond of guests at all times;
having acquired much wealth solely by his learning, pure of mind,

he once began to perform a great sacrifice.
A goat, its body adorned with worship, was brought for the purpose of immolation.

Laughing aloud, causing wonder to the world, it spoke [these] words:
"What [is gained] by these many sacrifices, even though performed according to rule,

yielding perishable fruits, and being the causes of birth, old age, and death?
Even after so much, O Brahmin, behold this state of mine!"

Hearing this speech of the goat, which aroused great curiosity,
the people residing in the erected sacrificial pavilion were struck with wonder.

Then, with folded hands and steady gaze,
the twice-born bowed, and full of faith, respectfully asked the goat.
The twice-born said: / What is your caste, what is your self, and what has happened to you? Tell me this. / Or by what action did you become a goat? Tell me the reason.
The goat said: / Long ago, I was in an exceedingly pure lineage of the twice-born, / an undertaker of hosts of sacrifices, and skilled in the knowledge of the Vedas.
Once, for the alleviation of our son's disease, / a goat was begged of me by my wife, who was bowed in devotion to Caṇḍikā.
Then, as it was being slain in the pavilion of Caṇḍikā, / the mother of that goat, an expounder of the Veda, cursed me:
“Because you, through an unscriptural path, wish to kill my son, O sinner, / lowest of the twice-born, you shall attain the womb of a goat!”
Then, having died in the course of time, I became a goat, O best of the twice-born, / after crossing through diverse torments and afflictions of wombs.
The brahmin said: / Even though you have entered an animal womb, you possess memory of past births. / My desire to hear of your lives is eager with the taste of curiosity.
The goat said: / Settle your mind, and I shall recount all of that to all these twice-born. / Once I became a monkey, through the training of a snake-charmer.
Seen by playing children as I danced in the courtyard of each house, / I saw my own generous wife and also my sons.
I turned away from the activity and abandoned the frenzy of dancing. / Thereupon the snake-charmer, with unbearable rounded sticks,
beat me violently, his eyes red with rage. / Then I fainted, blood streaming from my wounds in a flow.
Smelling food and water, I went to the state of death. / Then I became a dog, wandering from house to house,
filling my belly on the road, an eater of cast-off leftover food. / Once, inwardly desiring [food], I entered the kitchen of my own house.
Hungry, I wished to eat the cooked rice kept in the pot; / smelling the surface of the ground, looking slowly in the ten directions out of fear,
apprehensive of the sounds of people, and licking around on the side. / Then, at that time, having arrived, I was seen by my own sons
and by my old wife, and was beaten with clubs and the like. / Then, having my waist broken, shedding much blood,
I somehow went outside the house, overcome with faintness. / As my limbs smelled foul and became full of worms, in course of time,
I then attained the state of a wretched horse in the house of a liquor-distiller. / I became a horse, O wise one, and died here in the course of time.
Once I was brought by him to a public square crowded with people / for sale, stricken by old age, with my rows of teeth falling out.
By my wife, who was preparing once to make a pilgrimage to Dvārakā / and was seeking to buy a horse for a very small price,
I was bought by her with a rope, aged, for a small sum of money; / and she began to set out, mounting me together with two or three sons.
Slowly, slowly on the bank of a lake, I sank into thick mud; / there, with my neck twisted, I fell down into the mud.
Beaten repeatedly by the sons, whose hands held clubs and stones, / and being pulled up in various ways, I gave up my life's breaths.
Then, having determined that I was dead there, the sons, their efforts broken, / reproaching their wretched mother, turned back and went home.
Then, after dying, after a long time I went to the state of a goat, / having crossed through the torment and pain of many low and high wombs.
The twice-born said: / What use is this ceaseless series of sorrows, O great goat? / Tell me truly and directly how ultimate happiness may come to be.
The goat said: / I shall tell another wonder again, O twice-born, / to you who inquire peacefully, if you have curiosity.
There is a city named Kurukṣetra, bestowing liberation. / There ruled a king of the solar dynasty named Candraśarman.
At the time of a solar eclipse, filled with supreme faith, / he undertook to give the gift of a Kālapuruṣa.
Having summoned a twice-born who had crossed to the end of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, / he went with his priest to bathe in auspicious, sacred waters.
Then the Kālapuruṣa spoke aloud, as if laughing: / “Others do not accept even a minute thing in a sacred field;
at the time of a solar eclipse, in the place named Kurukṣetra, / how do you wish to accept the gift of a Kālapuruṣa, O twice-born?
Even knowing that this whole [matter] certainly brings about sin, / how do you proceed to act, with an intellect blinded by greed for wealth?”
Hearing these words of his, which caused astonishment to the world, / the twice-born said: “What is this fear of a great gift?
I indeed know well the means to cross over / this bottomless ocean of sin that is such a great gift.”
Then, having bathed and put on two garments, / pure, of cheerful heart, with white garlands and ointments,
holding the lotus-hand of the family priest standing by his side, / the ruler of the earth arrived, attended by people suitable for that occasion.
And having arrived, the king gave the Kālapuruṣa / according to the proper rite, with devotion, to that twice-born.
Splitting open the heart of the Kālapuruṣa, rising up mercilessly, / a certain sinful-souled Cāṇḍāla came forth, his eyes red.
Moreover, taking the opportunity in a festival of revelling in the slander of others, / a Cāṇḍāla woman of Slander approached the side of the twice-born's body.
This pair of Cāṇḍālas, having emerged with red eyes, / then violently made their way onto the body of the twice-born.
Repeating only the ninth chapter of the Gītā, dwelling in his heart, / while the king silently watched the twice-born trembling slightly,
the learned twice-born [resembled] the trembling ocean holding Govinda asleep within, / [moved] by the agitations of the wind, [now] an abode of sin.
Then, tormented by the Vaiṣṇava [beings] born from the syllables of the Gītā, / the pair of Cāṇḍālas fled, their efforts rendered futile.
That which was at the twice-born's side went forth with speed, / and that which had been existing in the body, delighting in revelling in the slander of others.
The king, having thus perceived the occurrence with his own eyes, / asked the twice-born, his eyes smiling with wonder:
“How was this dreadful, great calamity crossed over by you? / What mantra did you recite, O brahmin, or what god did you remember?
Who was that man, and who was that woman? How did they two appear, / and how did they attain pacification? Speak this to me, O twice-born.”
The twice-born said: / Having assumed the form of a Cāṇḍāla, [it was] dreadful sin incarnate; / and [the other was] slander in the form of a woman. I know these two.
The garland of mantras of the ninth chapter of the Gītā was remembered by me; / know all this to be its glorification, O lord of the earth.
I recite the ninth chapter of the Gītā every day, O king; / by that, the calamities arising from an improper acceptance of gifts were overcome.”
Having studied the ninth chapter from that twice-born, the king / and he—both of them attained supreme, excellent bliss.

6.184.m: The goddess said: / O omniscient one, consciousness of all, lord of all, guru of words! / Blessed am I, since I am looked upon by you, who are revered by Śiva,
as this sacred majesty of the ninth chapter has been expounded, / a nectar composed of stories sweet with many wonders.
Though I keep listening, O Lord of gods, satiety never arises in me; / my unblunted eagerness to hear only grows, O bull-bannered Lord!
The Gītā was born from the ocean of your greatness as the very life of the Vedas; / even there, the sages declared the tenth chapter to be foremost.

Tell me a narrative with reference to that great chapter!
Śiva said:
Listen, O fair-hipped lady, to the rare ladder to the citadel of heaven,
the supreme purifying tale that is, as it were, the culmination of all marvels! / In the city of Kāśī there was a brahmin devoted to meritorious fame,
calm-minded, free from violence, harshness, and reckless passion, / constantly engaged in cessation [of worldly activity] through mastery of the senses,
renowned as Dhīradhī, devoted to me like Nandin, / one who had crossed the ocean of the scriptures, skilled in the meaning of all sacred treatises.
Whenever he walked, his mind absorbed in deep meditation, / his intellect submerged in the inner self, possessing the vision of ultimate reality,
I would run with affection to give him the support of my hand. / Once, doing something wondrous, that thoughtful sage,
having sipped water, attaining a gaze abundant with supreme bliss fixed somewhat on the tip of his nose, / remained with his faculties as if asleep.
Resting his head upon the wide threshold of the door, O large-eyed lady, / he slept at night without fear, his eyes lowered for a moment.
Bhṛṅgiriṭin bowed to my lotus feet and asked me: / 'By what rite was your vision attained by him?
What asceticism did this great soul perform, what did he sacrifice, what did he chant, / that the god grants him the support of his hand at every step?
Why does he not manage to go outside this city? / Whenever he crosses the boundary of Kāśī by chance,
he does not see any embodied beings standing beside him. / I desire to know the cause of this as told by my master.
If I am worthy of grace, and if it is proper to speak, then tell me!' / Hearing this question of Bhṛṅgiriṭin, I spoke:
Once I was on Kailāsa, on its flank in a grove of punnāga trees, / in a grove full of clusters where celestial women with fair hips made sweet sounds,
where the quarters surged with the chatter of flocks of cuckoos, / filled with the cries of swarms of water-cocks, eagles, and other birds,
flecked with glistening drops from rotating wooden water-wheels, / delighting in shoots of plantains beside awakened watercourses,
inhabited by musk deer, enchanted by the melodies of Kiṃnaras, / frequented in places by deer whose corners of the eyes were sluggish with rumination,
crowded with swans teaching eloquence to parrots, / stirred by continuous breezes whistling from hollows,
where bees were intoxicated by liquor from the nectar of mādhavī blossoms, / overflowing with the fragrance of blooming triple-creeper flower-bunches,
with six-legged bees sluggish with the joy of the fragrance of fully blown bakula blossoms, / where the circle of the earth was washed by the nectar that sprang from the moon.
Having sat down upon an altar, I remained for a moment. / Then a fierce wind blew, shaking the shadow of the mountain,
with sprays from the tips of churning-sticks shattered by collisions with towering trees. / Afterwards arose a great roar that resounded across the slopes of the caves.

Then a certain bird descended from the vault of the sky, / having the hue of an autumn cloud, resembling a heap of collyrium,

Like a mass of darkness, or like a mountain whose wings had been severed,
the bird, resting on the lotus-filled ground, bowed down to me.
Bringing an unfaded lotus, he placed it at my feet. / Then that bird uttered a hymn of praise in clear speech:
'Victory to the God, the ocean of nectar of consciousness and bliss, Lord of the universe, / whose infinite form is a surge arising from the connection with eternal truth!
O you who are devoid of the three impurities through the thought of the impression of non-duality, / whose form is attained through profound absorption subject to conquered senses!
O unconditioned one, free [from all bounds], formless, beyond illness, / boundless, devoid of ego, unshielded, and beyond the qualities!
O you whose lotus feet are skilled in protecting those who take refuge, / who burned the Mind-born god with the flames of the great serpent that was a terrifying necklace!
O great all-pervading Lord who cleansed the earth struck down by the axe of the lord of Daityas, / O wiper of the dust of vermilion from the foreheads of the women of Tripura!
O you who are anointed with choice saffron from the lotus-like breasts of Kātyāyanī! / Homage to you who are far beyond means of knowledge, homage to you whose form is right comprehension!
Homage to the master of consciousness, homage to the one whose form is the three worlds! / I salute your lotus feet, kissed by the foremost of yogins,
the wonder for crossing beyond the shore of the boundless ocean of worldly existence! / Even Bṛhaspati lacks the boldness to praise you;
not even the thousand-faced Lord of Serpents has the skill / to describe you, O Mahādeva; who then am I, a bird of little intellect?'
Having heard this hymn of praise made by that winged creature, / I said to him: 'Who are you, bird, and from where have you come?
Your body resembles a swan, but your color is like a crow’s; / for what purpose have you come here? Let it be told!'

Thus questioned by me, the bird, his neck bowed in humility,
the bird, the foremost among those who know speech, spoke in gentle words:
'O Lord of gods, O Dhūrjaṭi, know me to be the swan of the Self-born Brahmā. / By a deed my present blackness has arisen, O all-pervading Lord.
Listen then, O all-knowing one, if what was asked is to be told: / having gone today from Lake Mānasa to the earth, I fell into distress.
Near the city of Saurāṣṭra, in a lake with blooming lotuses, / I took mouthfuls of lotus-fibers white like crescents of the young moon,
and summoning my strength, I quickly rose into the sky. / Then, from that sky, I suddenly fell to the earth.
Then, my mind overcome by delusion, my senses completely failing, / my body trembling from confusion, I was touched by cool breezes,
and awaking, seeing no cause for my own fall, [I thought:] / "Oh, what has befallen me today? How did my fall occur,
by which this blackness has come upon this body pale as ripe camphor?" / While I, filled with wonder, was thus reflecting,
I heard such a voice from a lotus: / "Arise, swan! I will explain the cause of your fall and your blackness."
Then, rising and approaching the middle of the lake, / I saw a charming lotus-cluster endowed with five lotuses.
I began to ask the cause of my blackness and my fall. / Then there I saw, standing in the atmosphere, six myriads of persons,
dark like clouds, clad in garments colored like gold, / four-armed, armed with mace, conch, discus, and lotus,
adorned with the brilliance of crowns, necklaces, armlets, and earrings. / Having bowed and circumambulated the lotus-plant with five lotuses,
because of that sin you fell onto the surface of the earth. / By that very [sin] blackness is seen on your body, O best of birds!
Seeing you fallen, with a mind filled with compassion, / this middle lotus spoke, and smelling its fragrance that arose,
sixty thousand bees went to heaven. / These whom you see, possessing the luster of blue water lilies,
were all the sons of a sage in their seventh past birth; / on the bank of this very lake, they practiced supreme asceticism."
Once there was an alluring woman whose breasts were like clusters of campaka blossoms, / whose dark side-glances were graceful, and who was filled with surging delight.
The radiance of her smile was touched by the moonlight of her nose-pearl; / placing a vīṇā upon her breasts, she sang sweetly in this forest.
Hearing the voice of the singing woman, the brāhmaṇas, like deer, / gathered near her and all gazed upon her at the same moment.
“She was seen by me; she is mine alone,” they said to one another. / Then among those brothers there arose a fight with fists.
With their chests crushed by one another’s fists, they lost their lives; / having experienced terrible hells, they became cranes on earth.
Then, they killed wild beasts and were burned by a forest fire; / then, having attained the state of elephants, they killed travelers on the road.
Having drunk poisoned water in the forest, they went to Yama’s abode; / having obtained births in succession as donkeys, camels, monkeys, and cats,
they were then born as bees and dwelt here in this lake; / today, having inhaled my fragrance, they attained the state of Viṣṇu.
Listen, O lord of birds, I shall explain the source of the glory that is in me: / in the third birth on earth prior to this birth,
I was the daughter of a twice-born named Sarojavadanā; / I was solely devoted to fidelity to my husband, intent on serving my elders.
Once, when I was delayed while teaching a myna bird, / I was cursed by my angry husband: “O wicked woman, become a myna!”
Having died and attained the state of a myna, by virtue of my fidelity to my husband, / a certain maiden nourished me in the hermitage of the sages.
There a brāhmaṇa recited in the morning the tenth chapter of the Gītā, renowned as the Vibhūti [chapter]; / I listened to that sin-destroying [recitation].
In time, having cast off the body of a myna, O bird, / through the glorification of the tenth chapter I became an apsaras in heaven,
renowned as Padmāvatī, a happy beloved of Padmā. / Once, as I was traveling through the sky in a celestial chariot,
beholding this delightful lake with its spotless lotuses, / as soon as I descended and began my water-sports,
just then Durvāsas arrived and saw me without clothes; / out of fear of him, I myself assumed this form of a lotus plant.

"With my two feet [I carry] two lotuses, and two with my two hands,
and the fifth lotus with my mouth; thus I am Pañcāmbujā."
Seen by that king of sages with eyes blazing in anger: / “O wicked woman, remain in this very form for a hundred years!”

"Having thus cast the curse, he vanished in an instant;
by the greatness of the chapter on divine manifestations, my voice does not fail."
Merely by flying over me you fell to the ground; / today is the end of my curse, as you remain [here], O best of birds.
Listen to the supreme chapter being sung by me, / merely by hearing which you shall be liberated this very day.

So he recited the tenth chapter with a smooth voice;
having heard it and having taken the lotus offered by her,
“The supreme lotus has been offered to you by me, the lotus plant” / —saying this, he cast off his body, and it was like a wonder.
Bhṛṅgiriṭi said: / Who was this sage-swan in his former birth, how did he become [such], / and for what reason did he cast off his body in front of you?

Having heard the words of Bhṛṅgiriṭi, I then said:
"In his previous birth, he was born in the house of a twice-born."
Renowned as Sutapas, he was a celibate student with senses conquered, / living in the household of his guru and daily studying the Veda.
And he performed service to his guru properly and with devotion; / [once,] while asleep, he touched with his foot the bed of his sleeping guru.
Because of that sin, he attained the state of an animal even in heaven; / then, the twice-born was born among the swans of Brahmā.
In this birth, in that very place, formerly up to the world of that [creator], / the tenth chapter of the Gītā was recited by a lotus.
Hearing it, the bird obtained unsurpassed knowledge of Brahman; / through the power of the tenth chapter, he was born here in a family of brāhmaṇas.
Owing to the practice in that birth, even from the lotus mouth of this child, / the tenth chapter of the Gītā always shines forth.
As a result of understanding its meaning, he always sees the God / bearing the conch and discus abiding within all beings.
Upon whichever embodied being his affectionate glance falls, / that person, even if a drinker of liquor or a slayer of a brāhmaṇa, becomes completely liberated.
Knowing that, the brāhmaṇa was brought by me, who am the embodiment of the Supreme Self, / to this city, which is by its very nature a place of liberation.
For the human beings here, liberation lies in the palm of their hand; / therefore, through the falling of his glance, no other special [change] is produced.
I do not permit him to go outside. The very difficult to attain knowledge of reality, / produced long ago through the majesty of the tenth chapter,
was obtained by this sage, as well as this living liberation; / therefore, as he moves and walks along the path, I give him my hand.
O Bhṛṅgiriṭi, great is this glory of the tenth chapter! / Thus was related in the presence of Bhṛṅgiriṭi that narrative.
This, which destroys all sins, has been told to you here. / A man or a woman, or whoever else it may be,
by the mere hearing of this, obtains the fruit of all stages of life.

6.185.m: The Goddess said: / This legendary history, O Lord, is the supreme means to the highest good. / Having heard it, full of compassion, a desire arises in me.
Relate the glorification of the eleventh chapter based upon a story, / O Virūpākṣa, O foremost of speakers, O Lord!
The Lord said: / Listen, O beloved, to the story connected with the description of the Gītā / and the purifying majesty of the [chapter] named the Cosmic Form.
O large-eyed lady, it is not possible to tell [all of] this chapter; / there are thousands of stories, [and] among them one is told by me.
On the bank of the river Praṇītā, there is a city known as Meghaṃkara, / an abode of greatness, with lofty surrounding walls and gate-towers,
adorned with golden pillars in the halls of spacious hermitages; / inhabited by prosperous, happy, peaceful men of good conduct, with senses subdued,
and horses; charming with beautiful crossroads; / adorned with courtyards and markets of gold radiant with jewelled pillars;
with the soft, sweet sound of clusters of ringing bells on banners; / with all the quarters resounded by the noise of the study of the Veda;
with the wide vault of the sky filled with the sounding of musical instruments; / with the heat dispelled by the breeze rising from the cloth of banners;
shining with the jingling of the anklets of women at the excellent gates of the royal highway, / with songs accompanied by lutes and flutes, and with the neighing of excellent steeds;
appearing, as it were, continually to vie with the cities of the guardians of the directions. / There abides, radiant, the Lord of the universe, who holds the Śārṅga bow in his hand,
the embodied supreme Brahman, the life of the eyes of the world, / the dignity of whose form is worshipped by the lotus eyes of Lakṣmī,
whose body is Trivikrama, dark like a raincloud, of gentle splendour, / his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, adorned with a lotus and a garland of forest flowers,
endowed with numerous ornaments like the ocean with jewels, / possessing a lustre like a dense cloud with a moving streak of lightning.
There in Mukuṭa dwells visibly the Supreme Person holding the Śārṅga bow; / having seen him, a creature is freed from the bond of worldly rebirth.
In that city there is a great holy site named Mekhalā, / where, having bathed, men constantly attain the realm of Viṣṇu.
Beholding there the Lord of the Universe, Narasiṃha, an ocean of compassion, / a man is freed from terrible sins accumulated across seven births.

Whichsoever man beholds the Lord of the Gaṇas at Mekhalā, / devoted to celibacy, self-controlled, devoid of possessiveness, free of egoism, / he always crosses over obstacles that are otherwise insurmountable.
In that Meghaṃkara, there was a certain most excellent brāhmaṇa, / known as Sunanda, skilled in the Vedas and Śāstras,
with the assemblage of senses subdued, devoted to Vāsudeva. / Beside the God holding the Śārṅga bow, O beloved,
he would recite this eleventh chapter of the Gītā, the display of the Cosmic Form; / through the power of that chapter he attained knowledge of Brahman.
Through absorption in praiseworthy consciousness filled with abundant supreme bliss, / having attained an unshakeable state with senses turned inward,
he remained constantly as a yogin liberated in life. / Once, when Jupiter was in the zodiac sign of Leo, that great yogin
