undertook to make a pilgrimage to the holy sites of the Godāvarī. / Arriving on the first day at the excellent holy site of Viraja,
beginning with the navel, he worshipped the deity at the holy sites, / and bathing again and again, he beheld Kamalā, the supporter of the world.
Having worshipped that Mahāmāyā, who bestows the fruit of all desires, / he then bathed at Tārātīrtha, and then at the confluence of the Kapilā;
he performed the eight-holy-sites rite, having offered libations to the ancestors; / having bowed to Śiva, the Lord of Kumārī, he went to Kapilādvāra.
Plunging in there, with sins from previous births cleansed away, / having worshipped, bowed to, and listened [to the praises of] the god Madhusūdana,

Having dwelt there for that night, he set out at dawn with the twice-born.
There, in the forest of Narasiṃha, at the tīrtha is Rāma's oblong reservoir,
where the Man-lion himself, worshipped by Prahlāda, abides.
Having seen that Lord of the gods of gods and worshipped him with devotion, / and spending that day there, he went to Ambikāpura.
By her grace toward devotees, Ambikā dwells there, / fulfilling all the desires of human beings.
Having worshipped Ambikā with devotion with flowers, fragrant unguents, / and various offerings, hymns of praise, and prostrations,
the brāhmaṇa went from that city to the town named Kaṇṭhasthāna, / where resides the supreme power, Mahālakṣmī of great splendour.
Having beheld her, whose orb of splendour is like the moon and the sun, / who carries the nectar of the lotus that cuts away the torment of cyclic existence,
who is served by the royal swan of the lotus heart of the king of yogins, / who consists of the great unproduced sound, whose form is non-dual,
having worshipped with a devotional disposition of mind the blessed Mahālakṣmī, / who bestows desired objectives, that lord of sages,
accompanied by the twice-born, reached the city of Vivāhamaṇḍapa; / in that city, he begged for a lodging in house after house.
The twice-born found no lodging to stay in any house; / a spacious residence was shown to him by the village protector.
Having entered, the brāhmaṇa lodged there along with his companions. / Then, at clear daybreak, that best of the twice-born, Sunanda,
looked outward from the lodging house, upon himself, / [and saw] where all the travelers had gone away by chance.
As he was walking, the village protector saw him approaching; / the village protector spoke to him: “You are long-lived in every way.
You are meritorious among fortunate men, and among the virtuous; / child, there is some extraordinary power within you.
Where have your companions gone? How is it you are outside that residence? / See that, O tiger among sages; I shall tell you [what happened] before you.
Indeed, I see no other ascetic equal to you here. / Do you know a great mantra? What science do you rely upon?
By the compassion of which deity is there extraordinary power in you? / Under the influence of that compassion, stay in this village, O best of brāhmaṇas.
O venerable one, I shall perform all service for you.” / Thus he made the lord of sages dwell in that village,
and served him with devotion day and night. / When seven or eight days had passed, he came
in the morning and wept before him, deeply afflicted: / “Today, for me who am bereft of fortune, my virtuous and devoted son
was devoured in the night by a rākṣasa with blazing fangs!” / When spoken to thus by the protector, that ascetic asked him:
“Where is that rākṣasa? How was your son devoured? Tell me.” / The village protector said: “There is a terrifying maneating night-wanderer in the city.
Coming constantly, he devours the men who inhabit the city. / Long ago he was implored here by all the citizens:
‘Protect us all, O rākṣasa! We shall provide food for you: / the travelers who sleep at night—devour them, O rākṣasa!’
Travelers made to enter this residence by the village protector / they provided as food to preserve their own lives.
You slept in that house along with other unfortunate men; / they were indeed devoured by him, but you were spared, O best of the twice-born.
You alone know your own power, O best of the twice-born. / Today, a friend of my son arrived.
Unknowingly, he too, my son's dear friend, / was made by me to enter that house along with other travelers.
Hearing that he had entered there, in the middle of the night my son / went to bring him back; he too was devoured by that rākṣasa.
Grieved, I spoke in the morning to that meat-eater: / ‘O wicked soul, my son too was devoured by you in the night.
Is there a means by which this son, sunk in your belly, / may live? Tell me, O night-wanderer!’
The rākṣasa said: ‘Not knowing that your son had entered within, I devoured him; / not knowing, that son of yours was devoured together with the travelers.
Even as he may live in my belly and be preserved, / that has also been ordained by the divine Creator.
If a twice-born constantly recites the eleventh chapter of the Gītā, / by its power I shall attain release, and the dead shall rise again.’
The village protector said: ‘How is there this wondrous power in the eleventh chapter?’
When asked thus by me, O brāhmaṇa, the night-wanderer spoke:
‘Long ago, as a certain vulture was flying through the path of the sky, / a piece of bone fell from the tip of its beak into some water.
A certain master of wisdom, coming then to that pool / and recognizing it as a great sacred site, performed the libation to the ancestors.
All the people said to him: “Tell us, how is this a sacred site?” / With his senses restrained, he would whisper the eleventh chapter at the three junctures of the day.
Having observed silence, that brāhmaṇa was killed on the road by thieves; / a fragment of his bone fell into the water from the vulture’s beak.
By that, this holy site arose, divine and destroyer of sins. / Then all those people bathed there in the reservoir;
and thus, freed from sin, they attained the supreme abode. / By the power of the eleventh chapter, there will be
liberation even for me, and also the resurrection of the travelers. / A certain brāhmaṇa who was vomited up by me stays right here;
and he was constantly reciting the eleventh chapter. / If that chief of vipras, having consecrated water seven times
with the mantra of that chapter, should throw it upon me, / then my release from the curse will come to pass, without a doubt.' / Thus instructed by him, I have come to your presence."
The vipra said: / "O guard, tell [me]: on account of what sin was that rākṣasa born, / because of which he devours sleeping men at night in that house?"
The village-guard said: / "Formerly in this village there was a certain vipra who was a farmer. / Once, the dvija was absorbed in protecting a field of rice.
Not far away, a great vulture devoured a traveler. / An ascetic, even from afar, felt pity to release him.

6.185.d:
भुक्त्वापांथंखगस्तावन्निरगादंबराध्वना
ततः स तापसः कोपात्तंबभाषेकृषीवलम्
धिक्त्वांहालिकदुर्बुद्धेकठोरमतिनिर्घृण
कुक्षिभरंपरत्राणविमुखंहतजीवितम् 78अं
6.185.m:
Having eaten the traveler, the bird then flew away along the path of the sky. / Thereupon that ascetic angrily addressed the farmer:

"Fie on you, wicked-minded plowman, cruel-hearted and ruthless,
interested only in filling your belly, indifferent to rescuing others, whose life is ruined!"
When people are attacked by thieves, by fanged beasts, by serpents, by enemies, fire, poison, and waters, / and by vultures, rākṣasas, bhūtas, vetālas, and the like,
one who, being capable, neglects them, incurs the fruit of their slaying. / A master who does not release a vipra seized by thieves and the like,
goes to a dreadful hell, and is born again as a wolf. / If someone says, "Let go, let go!" to one being slain in the forest,
afflicted by a vulture or a tiger, he attains the supreme state. / Those who are slain for the sake of cows by tigers, hunters, and wicked kings,
they too go to the abode of Viṣṇu, difficult to attain even for yogins. / Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeyas
do not equal a sixteenth part of protecting one who has sought refuge. / By neglecting a miserable, frightened living being,
even a meritorious person is cooked in Kumbhīpāka in the course of time. / Even seeing the traveler being devoured by the wicked vulture,
since you, though capable of warding [it] off, did not do so, / therefore, because you are merciless, you will become a night-wanderer.'
Hearing this curse of the sage, his body trembling, / bowing to the vipra, the plowman spoke plaintive words:
'With my eye cast far away here upon the protection of the field, / I did not notice this man nearby being killed by the vulture.
Therefore you ought to show mercy to me, a wretched man.' / The vipra said: / 'The one who knows the eleventh chapter and recites [it] day by day—
when water consecrated by him falls upon your head, / then your release from the curse will take place.'

Having said this, the ascetic departed, and the plowman became a rākṣasa. / Therefore, go, O best of the twice-born! Consecrate with that chapter / holy water and with your own hand cast it upon his head.
Mahādeva said: / Hearing that request of his, and filled with compassion, / saying "So be it," the sage went near the rākṣasa along with the guard.
Water consecrated by that yogic vipra with that eleventh [chapter], / which has the universal form, was thrown upon his head.
By the power of the Gītā chapter, he attained release from the curse. / Casting off the body of a rākṣasa, he then became four-armed.
Those travelers who had been swallowed by him by the thousands / became four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
They mounted celestial chariots. Just then, he spoke to the rākṣasa: / 'Which one is my son? O night-wanderer, show him to me!'
When the protector of the village had spoken thus, the rākṣasa, of celestial intellect, spoke: / "Know him to be four-armed in this manner, shining dark as a tamāla tree.
adorned with a ruby crown and divine jeweled earrings, / with broad shoulders charming with garlands, decorated with golden armlets,
lotus-eyed, handsome, with a lotus placed in his hand, / who has mounted a divine celestial chariot—your son who has attained godhood."
Hearing his words and seeing his son in such a state, / he began to lead him to his house; then that son laughed.
"How many times have you been born as my son, O guard? / Formerly I was your son; now I am a god.
I shall go to the Vaiṣṇava abode by the favor of the brāhmaṇa. / Look at even this night-wanderer who has obtained a four-armed body;
by the glorification of the eleventh [chapter], he goes to heaven together with the people. / Study that chapter from this vipra and recite it day and night;
there will be, without doubt, such a destination for you as well. / Therefore, father, association with the virtuous is difficult for people to obtain in every way.
Even if it has arisen for you today, accomplish your desired goal! / What is the use of riches, or enjoyment, or gifts? What is the use of sacrifices, or what of austerity?
What is the use of charitable works? The highest good comes from reciting the Universal Form, / the supreme form of Viṣṇu, and from hearing the chapter

that emerged from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa-Brahman, the mass of complete bliss, / for his friend Arjuna in Kurukṣetra—that elixir of absolute liberation,

And for men terrified of worldly existence, it removes the fear of mental pain and disease; / it destroys the suffering of many births. I see nothing else; remember that!
Śiva said: / Having spoken thus, he went along with all of them to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Then that village-guard studied that chapter from the vipra. / By its glorification, both of them went to the Vaiṣṇava abode.
Thus the story of the glorification of the eleventh [chapter] has been explained to you, / by merely hearing which grave sins are destroyed.

6.186.m: Mahādeva said: / "There is a city named Kolhāpura in the southern region, / an abode of happiness, O virtuous lady, the source of accomplishment for good people,
the supreme seat of the Supreme Śakti, attended upon by all the gods, / which is renowned in the Purāṇas as bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There are holy sites there by the crores, and Śiva lingas by the crores, / where there is Rudragayā, vast and world-renowned,
with radiant arched portals on the gateway towers of the great rampart like a lofty mountain, / where a lofty golden flag is on the summit of the palace-temple,
beautified by rows of rooftop pavilions of great mansions lustrous like the moon, / with regions of the directions scented by the smoke of incense pouring from latticed windows,

चलत्पताकविस्तीर्णच्छायंदेवालयान्वितम्
चतुरैः सुंदरैः स्निग्धैः श्रीमिद्भिःशुचि मानसैः
6.186.m: with the extensive shade of fluttering banners, furnished with temples of the gods; / inhabited by men who are clever, handsome, affectionate, glorious, pure-minded,
of good conduct, and richly ornamented; / and [by women] with fawn-like eyes, moon-like faces, curved locks of hair,
with the luster of blooming campaka flowers, full and lofty breasts, / slender waists, adorned with three folds above a deep navel,
broad hips, a pair of lovely shanks, excellent feet, / and jingling jeweled anklets with noisy girdles.
with rays shining from the nails of lotus hands bearing jingling bracelets, / where women dwell, intoxicating even the sages.
Furnished with every object, endowed with all enjoyments, / blessed with all auspicious things, accompanied by Mahālakṣmī—
there came a certain man, a youth, fair-complexioned and handsome-eyed, / with a conch-like neck, broad shoulders, a large chest, and mighty arms,
endowed with every auspicious mark, his mind intent on the sense-objects. / Entering the city, seeing the beauty on all sides in the mansions,
his mind was eager to see Mahālakṣmī, the queen of the gods. / Having bathed in the Maṇikuṇḍa and performed the libation to the ancestors,
having bowed to Mahālakṣmī, the great illusion, he praised her with devotion: / "Victorious is the Mother of the Universe, refuge [to all], of boundless compassion,
bringing about the birth, protection, and destruction of the universe with a glance! / Empowered and commanded by her power, that Parameṣṭhin creates [the worlds];
taking support of that very power, Acyuta protects the universe; / entered into by that power, Hara destroys everything.
I worship that supreme power, exalted in creation, preservation, and dissolution, / whose lotus feet are meditated upon by yogins, O Kamalā, O abode of lotuses!
You apprehend all natures, our sense-objects; / you alone are the web of constructs, and you make the mind of that nature.
Your form is will, knowledge, and action; your essential nature is supreme consciousness; / partless, stainless, eternal, formless, unblemished,
unbroken, free from distress, without support, free from affliction— / who indeed is capable of describing your greatness in this way?
I revere [you] who pierce the six cakras and sport within the twelve-petaled [lotus], / consisting of the unstruck sound, having the nature of the bindu, nāda, and kalā.
O Mother, stream of nectar dripping from the full, cool-rayed moon, / O affectionate one, you nourish children such as Sanaka and others, the sky-clad ones.
Inwoven as auspicious consciousness in waking, dream, and deep sleep, / existing in the fourth [state], at the junctions of compassion and truth,
you constantly give to living beings all the treasures of Brahman. / Withdrawing the collection of principles, by you, who transcend the fourth [state],
identity with the prototype is granted to yogins without distinction. / I bow to [you as] Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and also Vaikharī.
O Goddess, you assume forms for the sake of protecting the universe: / you are Brāhmī, and you are Vaiṣṇavī, and you are Māheśī, O Ambikā!
You are Vārāhī, you are Mahālakṣmī, you are Nārasiṃhī, you are Aindrikā; / you are Kaumārī, you are Caṇḍikā, you are Lakṣmī, the purifier of the universe.
You are Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Universe; you are Śaśinī and Rohiṇī; / you are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, you indeed are the nectar, O Parameśvarī!
O you adorned with mighty arms that severed the club-like arms of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, / whose eyes rolled from drinking the blood dripping from Raktabīja,
with a pair of mature arms that uprooted the neck of the frenzied Mahiṣa, / whose valour arrived for the slaughter of the great Daitya Śumbhāsura!
O you of infinite deeds, praise be to you, O Mother of the three worlds! / O wish-granting creeper to devotees, be gracious to me, O Parameśvarī!"
Puffed with praise by him in this manner, the goddess Mahālakṣmī then herself, / assuming her own form, spoke to that man:
Śrī Lakṣmī said: / "O prince, I am pleased; choose an excellent boon!" / The prince said: / "My father, a protector of the earth, while undertaking a great sacrifice, a horse sacrifice,
was seized by disease through the power of fate and went to heaven. / Then, his body having been preserved in hot oil by me,
and placed there, that sacrifice proceeded just as before. / Then the sacrificial horse, having traversed the circuit of the earth, [fastened] to the post,
broke its tether at midnight and was taken away somewhere by someone. / Seeing that it was nowhere to be found, when the people turned back, I,
having taken leave of all the priests, came to you for refuge. / If you are pleased, O Goddess, then let that sacrificial horse of mine
be found, so that this sacrifice may be completed, / and thereby freedom from debt will come to my father, the king.
Act accordingly, O sustainer of the universe, affectionate to those who seek refuge!" / The Goddess said: / "At my doorway is a twice-born, an ascetic known as Samādhi.
By my command, he will accomplish all your tasks." / Having been thus addressed by Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the prince then
came to where the sage, the ascetic Samādhi, stood. / Having bowed to his lotus feet, he stood with folded hands.
Then the brāhmaṇa said to him: "You have been sent by the Mother. / I shall accomplish all this that you desire; behold!"
Having spoken thus, the possessor of mantras drew forth all the thirty [gods]; / then that son of the king saw the gods.
with folded hands, their bodies trembling. / Then the best of the twice-born addressed all those immortals:
"The horse intended for the sacrifice of this prince / has been stolen and carried off at night by the king of the gods.
O gods, bring his horse at once!" / Then, by the word of that sage, the sacrificial horse was
surrendered by the gods; then, dismissed by him, those dwellers of heaven [departed]. / Having seen the gods summoned and having recovered the lost horse,
the son of the lord of the earth bowed and spoke these words to that sage: / "A wonder is this power of yours, O best of ṛṣis!
This extraordinary feat was performed by you: summoning the thirty [gods] in an instant! / Seizing it from their hand, you have given me this sacrificial horse.
There is nothing else so difficult to perform, even for the gods, / that you alone will not be capable of doing, and no one else.
Listen, O brāhmaṇa: Bṛhadratha, a protector of the earth, was my father. / Having begun a horse sacrifice, he met his end through fate.
Even today his body remains, preserved in hot oil. / You ought to restore him to life once more, O best of men!"
Hearing this, that great sage smiled and said: / "Let us go there where your father's sacrificial pavilion is."
Then, having arrived there along with him, that ascetic, by contemplation, / consecrated water with mantras and poured it upon the head of that corpse.
Then the king regained consciousness, rose up, and looked around. / That lord of the earth asked that foremost of the twice-born: "Who are you, O righteous one?"
Then the king's son related everything to the protector of the earth. / Having bowed to that brāhmaṇa who had restored his life,
the king said: "By what merit is there this extraordinary power in you, / by which life was given to me and the dwellers of heaven were summoned,
and the sacrifice rescued, O brāhmaṇa? Explain this to me!" / Addressed thus by him, that brāhmaṇa spoke with a gentle voice:
"I recite the twelfth chapter of the Gītā without indolence; / by that comes this power, O king, through which you have obtained life."
Having heard this, that king recited the excellent twelfth chapter / in the presence of that brāhmaṇa-seer, accompanied by brāhmaṇas.
By the majesty of that chapter, they all attained a good realm; / and having recited it, other souls also attained supreme liberation, ah!
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the glorification of the Gītā, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].
